title: mTLS & Zero-Trust Networking in a Mesh
summary: How a mesh enforces service identity and encryption at the infrastructure layer — the mechanics behind zero-trust networking.

slides.markdown:
**Zero-trust** means the network itself is never trusted — every caller proves who it is, every time, even inside your own datacenter.

- **mTLS** is the mechanism: both sides present a certificate, not just the server.
- A mesh's control plane issues and rotates those certificates automatically.
- mTLS proves **identity** — it does not, by itself, decide what an identity is **allowed** to do.

slides.subTitle: Never trust the network, always verify the caller
slides.markdown:
Traditional network security assumed a **perimeter**: anything inside the firewall was trusted by default. Zero-trust rejects that assumption entirely — being on the internal network proves nothing, so **every** call, internal or external, must independently prove its identity.

This shift matters because a perimeter model fails completely the moment an attacker gets one foothold inside — from there, everything was implicitly trusted. Zero-trust removes that free lateral movement by requiring proof at every single hop.

slides.subTitle: Both sides prove identity, not just the server
slides.markdown:
In ordinary TLS (the padlock in your browser), only the **server** proves its identity with a certificate — the client stays anonymous at the TLS layer. **Mutual TLS (mTLS)** requires **both** sides to present and verify a certificate, so the server also cryptographically confirms who's calling it.

In a mesh, this happens entirely between sidecars — the application never handles certificates itself. Every service-to-service call is both encrypted **and** identity-verified in both directions, transparently.

slides.subTitle: How a mesh assigns and verifies who's calling
slides.markdown:
Rather than identity tied to an IP address (which changes constantly with Pod churn), a mesh assigns identity to a **workload** — typically a SPIFFE-style identity like `spiffe://cluster/ns/orders/sa/orders-sa`, encoding namespace and service account. The mesh's control plane acts as a **certificate authority**, issuing a short-lived cert per workload identity.

Because identity is tied to the workload's role, not a fragile network address, it survives restarts, rescheduling, and IP changes — the cert always says "I am the orders service," regardless of which node or IP it's currently running on.

![A mesh-enforced mTLS handshake between two sidecars](assets/mtls-handshake.svg)

Both sidecars present their workload certificate and verify the other's against the mesh's certificate authority — entirely before the application-level request is forwarded. The applications on either end never see this exchange; they just make and receive plain HTTP calls locally to their own sidecar.

slides.subTitle: During migration
slides.markdown:
| Mode | Behavior |
|---|---|
| **Permissive** | Accepts both mTLS and plaintext connections on the same port |
| **Strict** | Rejects any connection that isn't mTLS |

Permissive mode exists specifically for **migration**: it lets you onboard services onto the mesh gradually, since a service not yet running a sidecar can still connect in plaintext while you roll the mesh out. Only after every caller has a sidecar do you flip to strict — flipping too early breaks any straggler still connecting in plaintext.

slides.subTitle: Locking down from permissive to strict without an outage
slides.markdown:
A team enables the mesh in **permissive** mode across 40 services, so nothing breaks while sidecars roll out one deployment at a time. Before flipping to strict, they check mesh telemetry for any connections still arriving in **plaintext** — this surfaces two legacy batch jobs still running outside the mesh entirely.

Only after those two jobs are either migrated onto the mesh or explicitly exempted does the team switch the namespace to **strict** mTLS — flipping first would have silently broken both jobs the moment plaintext connections started being rejected.

slides.subTitle: mTLS alone isn't authorization
slides.markdown:
mTLS proves **who's calling** (authentication) — it says nothing about **what they're allowed to do** (authorization). A common mistake: assuming that because mTLS is enforced mesh-wide, any service can safely call any other service, since "they're all verified."

Verified identity plus **no authorization policy** just means every authenticated service can call every other authenticated service — real zero-trust also needs explicit authorization rules (e.g. "only `checkout` may call `payments`") layered on top of the identity mTLS establishes.
